title: Graceful Surge Proxy & Latency Budget Controller - PRD sketch
content:
Summary:

This is a working PRD sketch for a unified runtime component we are calling the Graceful Surge Proxy (GSP) + Latency Budget Controller (LBC). The goal: enable Dedicated customers to tolerate short-lived demand spikes without violating tail latency SLOs or requiring large permanent capacity reservations.

Why this (problem statement):
- Customers running dedicated pools face unpredictable microbursts (cron jobs, seasonal traffic, experiments) that either force them to over-reserve capacity or suffer degraded tail latency.
- Existing burst options (manual warm pools, hard preemption) are brittle: either costly or cause noisy neighbor impacts and poor UX (failed requests, timeouts).
- We need an operator-visible, SLO-aware proxy layer that mediates incoming requests, applies per-tenant latency budgets, and orchestrates safe burst strategies (soft preempt, borrow warm slots, degrade model fidelity) with clear observability and rollback paths.

Success metrics (what success looks like):
- 30–50% reduction in committed reserved GPU hours for customers with <10% monthly burst time, without increasing 99th percentile latency beyond SLO by >10%.
- Measurable reduction in token-level cost during steady state thanks to smaller base reservations and smarter warm pools.
- <2% increase in customer-visible 500 errors during controlled rollouts compared to baseline.
- Operator: ability to see per-tenant latency budget consumption and a clear audit trail for fallback actions.

User stories / personas:
- Platform engineer at scale SaaS: "I want my Dedicated pool to autoscale for predictable daily load but still survive unpredictable spikes without paying for large 24/7 reserve."
- ML infra owner: "I want to degrade model fidelity automatically (quantized variant or 2nd-best model) when the latency budget is exhausted instead of returning 504s."
- Customer SRE: "I need transparent accounting for burst consumption and an SLA-safe way to opt into different burst tiers."

Non-goals:
- Replacing long-term committed capacity contracts or billing model changes. This is an operational/inference control layer, not a pricing product.
- Full multi-cloud scheduling or replacing low-level GPU allocator. We integrate with existing Dedicated autoscaler and scheduler hooks.

High-level design (sketch):
1) Graceful Surge Proxy (GSP):
   - Sits in front of per-tenant request routing for Dedicated pools. Lightweight, per-request decision point.
   - Maintains per-tenant state: latency budget tokens, active fallbacks, warm-slot pointers, soft-preempt counters.
   - Implements short-circuit policies: queue-with-deadline, route-to-fallback-model, serve-from-cache, or fail-fast with graceful error payload.

2) Latency Budget Controller (LBC):
   - Aggregates historical request latency distributions and SLOs per tenant and per model.
   - Computes a sliding latency budget (ms * requests) and exposes an API for GSP to query budget availability.
   - Suggests fallback policies ranked by estimated quality loss and cost savings (e.g., quantized model, smaller context length, cached response).

3) Burst Strategies (orchestrated by GSP + autoscaler hooks):
   - Warm-Pool Borrow: ephemeral warm slot lease (soft allocation) for X minutes. Leases are best-effort and revocable.
   - Burst Credits: tenancy maintains a small monthly/weekly credit balance; credits convert to temporary concurrency shares during spikes.
   - Fidelity Degrade: automatic downgrade to lighter variants (int8/4bit or distilled models) at request time when budget is low.
   - Queue-and-Serve with Deadline: short queue (e.g., 200ms) before applying fallbacks; queue length and deadline are per-tenant and tied to budget state.
   - Soft Preemption: defer low-priority background requests (e.g., batched embedding jobs) in favor of latency-bound traffic.

Policy layers and controls (customer-facing + operator):
- Tiered Burst Profiles: customers select tiers (none, conservative, balanced, aggressive). Each tier maps to parameters: max soft-lease minutes, allowed fidelity reduction, credit burn rate.
- Isolation knobs: shard affinity (pin heavy tenants to slices), concurrency caps, priority classes, and a noisy-neighbor score that triggers temporary hard isolation.
- Emergency failover lane: if budget is exhausted and no fallbacks possible, route to a degrade-only region or return an enriched error describing why (so downstream can degrade gracefully).

Autoscaling integration points:
- Hook: GSP emits signals to Dedicated autoscaler: warm-pool demand estimate, predicted short-term RPS, and credit depletion events.
- Prewarm policy: autoscaler can prewarm nodes based on aggregate soft-lease demand across tenants when predicted utility > threshold.
- Backpressure feedback loop: when autoscaler cannot honour prewarm requests, GSP increases fidelity-degrade and backoff durations; metrics emitted to operators.

Observability & telemetry: what we need to show on Console:
- Per-tenant latency budget usage (time-series), burn rate, projected exhaustion time.
- Per-tenant fallback events (counts, types), warm-lease grants/denials, preemption incidents.
- Cost delta estimates when using warm-pool vs fidelity degrade.
- Causal traces: request-level annotation showing decisions taken by GSP and which fallback model served the response.
- Alerting: budget burn > x% in y minutes, warm-lease grant failure rate > z%.

Operational runbook (early operator notes):
- During rollout, default to conservative tier for existing Dedicated customers; allow opt-in for balanced/aggressive via Console toggle.
- If noisy neighbor detected (beyond threshold), auto-isolate tenant to a quarantine slice and open Slack alert to infra-oncall channel.
- Rollback: disable GSP routing for a tenant (instant) and revert to existing hard-eviction/autoscaler behavior.

Security & compliance considerations:
- Fallback models must respect data residency flags (no cross-region degrade unless tenant allowed).
- Audit log for all decision points (which fallback used, which warm-lease allocated).
- KMS usage for any model keys or private artifacts remains unchanged.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal alpha): GSP + LBC prototype behind feature flag on small Dedicated pool. Manual acceptance tests (latency regressions, fallback correctness). (~4 weeks)
- Phase 1 (pilot customers): Opt-in for 5 pilot tenants from varied profiles (high RPS, bursty, enterprise). Collect metrics for 8 weeks, tune tier defaults. (~8 weeks)
- Phase 2 (gradual rollout): Default-enable conservative tier for new Dedicated tenants; allow existing tenants to opt-in. Monitor cost and tail-latency KPIs. (~6–10 weeks)

Open questions / risks (TODOs):
- Quantifying quality loss: need eval harness that maps fidelity-degrade choices to a quality delta per customer workload. (Action: product + applied-ml to design prompt-set based evals)
- Billing UX: how to expose burst credit consumption and invoicing for aggressive tiers. Finance involvement required.
- Warm-lease fairness: how to prioritize leases across tenants during correlated global spikes. Could use proportional share or priority-lane auctions.
- Cold-start cost: prewarming reducing cost gains if overused. Need threshold logic to prevent thrashing.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- (Aisha) Draft API spec for GSP <-> autoscaler signals (req/response shapes, rate limits). Target: 2024-11-22.
- (Mateo) Prototype LBC budget computation job that ingests 30-day P99 latency windows and exposes REST API. Target: 2024-11-29.
- (Evelyn + Ravi) Work with Applied ML to list candidate fallback variants per model family and estimate quality delta. Target: 2024-12-06.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally high-level and operational; we need infra and applied-ml buy-in before writing detailed SLO maths. Please annotate sections with specific implementation concerns or missing integrations (scheduler, prewarm API limits).
- Related tickets: JIRA:DEDICATED-783 (proto), DEDICATED-789 (pilot), DEDICATED-801 (console telemetry).

Appendix (sketch of latency-budget concept):
- Budget = target_p99_ms * target_qps * window_seconds. Subtract observed latency consumption measured as sum(latency_ms * requests) for recent window -> remaining budget. When remaining budget < threshold, trigger fallbacks.
- We will refine with percentiles and request-weighting (e.g., large-context requests cost more).

Quick UX mocks + console controls (notes):
- Toggle: Burst profile (None | Conservative | Balanced | Aggressive) with hoverable estimated monthly cost delta and expected impact on p99.
- Time-series: Budget remaining %, projected exhaustion time, and last fallback reason chart.
- Audit: expandable list of fallback events with links to traces and logs.

End of sketch.

-- Aisha
